elements.quote: However, studies assessing their effectiveness in delivering primary prevention interventions for non-communicable disease prevention and control in LMIC settings are limited,[10] though this has been proven for developed countries.[11] Further, whatever sparse results are available are mostly through observational studies and evidence from controlled trials needs to be synthesised.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge (limited studies in LMIC settings, proven in developed countries) and the uncertainty (need to synthesize evidence from controlled trials).

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state the need for the review due to the deficiency in available effectiveness parameters for CHW-delivered NCD interventions in developing countries.

elements.quote: Only four systematic reviews assessing this effectiveness in LMIC/ developing countries could be identified after review of published literature.[11-14]
elements.reason: The authors acknowledge the existence of four previous systematic reviews, which establishes the context for why their review is needed (to address the deficiency in effectiveness parameters).
The review focuses on the effectiveness of a workforce (Community Health Workers) rather than a specific pharmacological or clinical intervention with a defined mechanism of action.
The manuscript does not present a logic model, and while it discusses CHW interventions, it does not explicitly use a logic model to describe the relationships between components and outcomes.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors. This was conducted following the hypothesis that for NCD control programs employing a community health worker is more likely to be successful than routine care.
elements.reason: The review objectives are stated, but they are not formulated using a formal question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, SPIDER, etc.).

elements.quote: Table 1. Methodological characteristics of included trials. ... Intervention ... Control ... Primary Outcomes
elements.reason: The review is of intervention effects, and the planned comparisons (Intervention vs. Control) are clearly structured and presented in Table 1, which serves as an appropriate variant of a PICO framework.

elements.quote: A research was considered eligible for inclusion if it followed a randomised controlled study design in community settings of low middle income countries with community health worker as intervention delivery person for general or high risk population for primary prevention of NCDs as compared to routine care or enhanced routine care as comparator.
elements.reason: The review explicitly specifies the study design (randomised controlled trials), setting (community settings in low-middle income countries), population (general or high-risk for NCDs), intervention (CHW-led), and comparator (routine care or enhanced routine care).

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review... without restriction to language... Unpublished reports identified in a database or referenced in a publication in the initial search were also read.
elements.reason: The review specifies the publication date range (2000-2015), language policy (no restriction), and inclusion of unpublished reports.

While the review mentions excluding studies and provides a table of excluded studies, it does not explicitly state a policy or distinction regarding whether studies were excluded because outcomes were not measured versus because results were not reported.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were carried out separately for each outcome and type of study design (RCT/ cRCT).
elements.reason: The review specifies that studies were grouped for synthesis by outcome and by study design (RCT vs cRCT).

elements.quote: The time period was limited to base evidence on recently conducted studies in light of recent shift in delivery of primary health care services towards NCDs in most of the developing countries.
elements.reason: The review provides a clear rationale for the restriction on the publication time period (2000-2015).

elements.quote: Searches of published literature on effectiveness of NCD control interventions delivered through community health worker under the programme (focus on developing countries) were done in the following biomedical, and general reference electronic databases, without restriction to language: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015)
elements.reason: The text specifies the search period (2000-2015) for the databases searched.

elements.quote: Searches of published literature on effectiveness of NCD control interventions delivered through community health worker under the programme (focus on developing countries) were done in the following biomedical, and general reference electronic databases, without restriction to language: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library.
elements.reason: The names of the databases are provided (PubMed, EMBASE, OVID, WHO library, Cochrane library) and the coverage dates (2000-2015) are provided for the first three. However, the search interface or platform is not explicitly specified for all, and coverage dates are missing for the WHO and Cochrane libraries.

elements.quote: Results of our review are in concordance with that of a Cochrane review by Uthman et al in 2015 which assessed the effects of multiple risk factors intervention for primary prevention of CVDs.[14] Ebrahim in 2011 had also demonstrated similar results.[52] However both these reviews did not focus on the role of CHW as a change agent. Recently two reviews focussing upon this concept have been published [12, 13] but both of these lacked quality of evidence.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly compares the results of the current review with other relevant evidence (Cochrane review by Uthman et al., Ebrahim, and two other recent reviews), discussing concordance and differences in focus/quality.

elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. A probable reason could have been the nature of studies (community based studies, as against controlled clinical settings) which dilutes the effect of interventions due to within subject and within cluster differences. Implementation of interventions by less trained staff could also have contributed to a decrease in effect size. Most of the trials reported training the health workers in a workshop or a short course, which could also have affected the performance. With the exception of a trial by Jafar et al, all other included trials relied on short-term effects of interventions and failed to report issues related to behaviour relapse... Also, shorter length of follow ups fail to capture 'saturation effects' of primary prevention interventions implemented at population level.
elements.reason: The discussion section explicitly identifies and discusses several limitations of the included evidence, such as low magnitude of effect, low quality of evidence, the nature of community-based studies, implementation issues, short-term follow-ups, and failure to report behavior relapse.

elements.quote: Minor and major methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence should also be understood while interpreting the results of this review. As we combined the results of individual and cluster randomised controlled trials, suitable analytical methods were used to make the trial results comparable. Second, the settings in which the trials were conducted varied despite developing country settings. The type of CHW, nature of interventions also were not exactly similar. The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable PLOS heterogeneity in evidence.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly discuss methodological challenges encountered during the synthesis of evidence, such as combining different study designs (individual and cluster RCTs) and managing heterogeneity.

elements.quote: We tried to address this by use of a 'maximum 75% heterogeneity cut-off criteria' for selection of results of risk factors for pooling.
elements.reason: The authors discuss the impact of the identified heterogeneity (a limitation of the synthesis process) and describe the specific methodological step taken to mitigate this impact (the 75% cut-off criteria).

elements.quote: The evidence suggests that the CHWs may be effective in altering the risk factors for NCDs for people in developing countries. While community health workers' led interventions were not very successful in altering individuals' behaviour patterns, modifications in physical parameters, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure was clearly observed. Community health workers were also able to introduce and sustain a long term control on HbA1C levels among diabetics
elements.reason: The discussion section explicitly interprets the findings regarding the effectiveness of CHWs in clinical practice (e.g., blood pressure and HbA1C control).

elements.quote: As countries turn towards universal healthcare coverage, policymakers will need high quality evidence about efficient strategies for NCDs, particularly those focusing on prevention, to avoid burdening health systems with large numbers of individuals with chronic conditions that are expensive to treat. ... So, in this sense, a process of task shifting will be required in order to extend services to those who need them in the face of a shortage of physicians, nurses, and other higher-level health professionals.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly addresses policy implications, specifically regarding universal healthcare coverage, task shifting, and resource allocation for NCD prevention.

elements.quote: The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke. This gap in information needs to be filled, which requires further research using robust trial designs and longer follow-up periods. More good quality trials need to be designed and implemented to study the effects of interventions. Measurement approaches should be made more objective and reliance on self-reported parameters should be reduced in order to enhance methodological robustness of the trials.
elements.reason: The discussion provides clear, explicit recommendations for future research, including the need for more trials in specific disease areas (cancer, COPD, stroke), the need for robust designs, longer follow-up, and more objective measurement approaches.
